overview: AI Operations is where AI meets day-to-day control: the data a model learns from, how it is built, changed, supervised and tested, how it can be attacked, and what happens when it fails. It is the largest AAIA domain. The IS auditor applies familiar control areas, such as change, access and incident management, to systems that behave differently: models learn from data, drift over time and can be steered through their inputs.
analogy: Think of a busy restaurant kitchen with a talented but unpredictable chef. The ingredients matter as much as the recipe (data), each new dish is tasted before service (testing and stage gates), and changing a sauce counts as a menu change even if the recipe card looks the same (AI change management). A head server watches what reaches the tables and can send a plate back (human oversight). Suppliers are checked for tampered produce (poisoning and supply chain). When a guest falls ill, the kitchen stops serving that dish, keeps samples and finds the cause (incident response). The auditor is the inspector, never the cook.

topics.overview: AI learns from data, so data controls are model controls. This topic covers where training and retrieval data come from and whether it may be used, whether it is accurate and representative of the people a model will serve, and how training, validation and test sets are kept apart so reported results can be trusted.
can_do: Trace a model's training data back to its source and its rights to use
Spot unrepresentative or poorly labeled data before it becomes biased decisions
Recognize leakage between training and test data and what it does to reported results

subtopics.name: Data Provenance, Lineage and Rights to Use
subtopics.definition: Data provenance is the documented origin of data; lineage traces how it changed on the way to a model; rights to use confirm it may lawfully be used for training.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A model inherits every flaw in its data: errors, bias, unlicensed content or planted records. Without lineage, nobody can show the data was fit and lawful, or trace a bad output to its cause.
how_it_works: Each dataset, and each record gathered under changing terms, carries its source, owner, date, license or consent basis and use limits, which reach trained models.
Lineage records every transformation, such as cleaning, labeling, joining and sampling, and which supplied values were estimated, so each model version traces to an exact snapshot.
Third-party, open and model-generated data need the same evidence; a broker's warranty is not provenance, and model output terms may bar training on generated data.
Documents used for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) need an owner, matching access rights and licenses covering every audience; separate indexes keep clients apart better than tags.
Pipelines check integrity, such as approved sources and file hashes, so unexpected or tampered records are caught before training.
subtopics.example: Priya, a data owner at a Canadian public library network, wants to train a book-recommendation model on borrowing histories and a purchased set of reader reviews. The review vendor cannot say whether reviewers agreed to reuse. The IS auditor traces both sources through the lineage records and reports that the review data has no documented right to use.

review: Trace a sample of training records to their documented source and license
Compare the lineage log with the data snapshot named for the deployed model
Inspect third-party data agreements for rights to train and use limits
evidence: System-generated lineage records for the deployed model's training data
Data source register with owner, origin and legal basis
Third-party data licenses and supplier provenance statements
audit_focus.recommend: Have data owners record provenance and rights for every dataset and block unverified data from training pipelines.
audit_focus.decides: The data owner approves use; management accepts any residual data risk within the board-approved risk appetite

subtopics.isaca_rule: No provenance, no training. Data whose origin, rights or integrity cannot be shown is not fit to feed a model. Ask for origin and rights evidence before quality tests, and hold third-party data to the internal standard.

exam_traps.trap: A supplier's warranty that its data is accurate is enough to use it for training.
exam_traps.why: A warranty is a vendor claim. It does not show origin, consent or freedom from tampering, and cannot be traced when a model misbehaves.

key_terms.definition: The recorded path of data from its source through every transformation into a model or report.
A design in which a generative model looks up documents at answer time and uses them in its response.
A provider's conditions on how content its model generates may be used, including whether it may train other models.

subtopics.memory_aid: Where from, who owns it, may we use it: then train.

subtopics.name: Data Quality, Labeling and Representativeness
subtopics.definition: Data quality for AI means training data is accurate, complete, consistently labeled and representative of the people and conditions the model will meet in use.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A model reproduces its data's patterns. Mislabeled or one-sided data produces confident but wrong or unfair decisions, often hurting underrepresented groups.
how_it_works: Labels need written guidelines, trained labelers and agreement checks, where wide splits signal unclear rules; model-prefilled labels inherit its errors; rewarding an outcome skews labels.
Representativeness compares the data's people, places and conditions with those served; opt-in groups and outcomes shaped by a device absent in use may differ.
Historical data and proxy targets, such as spending standing in for need, carry past bias and access gaps, which the model learns and repeats.
More data of the same kind, copies included, does not fix a skewed mix; targeted collection or reweighting does, but neither restores outcomes nobody reported.
Data fitness is rechecked in production, as populations change; an anomaly model learns whatever its training window held as normal, slow-building attacks included.
Dropping records that lack a label can remove the outcomes a model most needs when the label is missing because of that outcome, such as cases that ended early.
subtopics.example: A Kenyan microinsurance firm builds a crop-claims model from claim photos labeled by two contractors. Spot checks show the contractors disagree on a third of the photos, and almost none come from the dry northern counties the product will cover. The IS auditor reports both gaps to the product owner before validation.

review: Compare group shares in the training data with current customer or user records
Reperform labeling on a sample and measure agreement with recorded labels
Inspect data quality rules and exception reports for the training pipeline
evidence: Population comparison showing each group's share in data and in use
Labeler agreement statistics and labeling guidelines
Data quality exception reports with resolution status
audit_focus.recommend: Have the model owner set representativeness and labeling criteria and close data gaps before validation.
audit_focus.decides: The model owner decides whether the data is fit for purpose

subtopics.isaca_rule: Judge data against its use: who will the model decide about, and are they in the data? Representativeness and label quality come before volume.

exam_traps.trap: Adding more data will fix bias in a model.
exam_traps.why: More data with the same skew repeats the same gap. Fix the mix with targeted data, then test results by group.

key_terms.definition: The correct answer attached to a training example, such as fraud or not fraud, that a model learns to predict.
How closely the data's mix of people and conditions matches the population the model will serve.
Unfairness built into past decisions or records that a model learns and repeats.
Bias from training only on cases a past decision let through, such as hired applicants; outcomes for those turned away are never recorded.

subtopics.name: Training, Validation and Test Separation
subtopics.definition: Data separation splits data into a training set the model learns from, a validation set used to tune it, and a test set kept unseen for the final check.
subtopics.why_it_matters: If test data overlaps training data, the model is graded on answers it has seen, so reported accuracy overstates performance.
how_it_works: Splits are made and recorded before modeling; the test set stays apart from builders and tested vendors, and keeps the cases models fail.
Leakage means a person or record on both sides of a split, or inputs holding later facts, such as scores recalculated after the outcome; store inputs as received.
Each customer's records stay on one side; splitting by person, not by row, prevents hidden overlap.
Out-of-time testing holds back the latest period, showing whether the model works on later data; classes collected differently can teach shortcuts that same-pool tests miss.
No unseen check comes from tuning on the test set, public benchmarks a large model may have learned, or records an earlier version trained on.
Steps that learn from or copy data, such as input selection, outcome averages, augmentation, generator fitting or copying another model's scores, run after the split, on training data only.
subtopics.example: A Brazilian logistics firm predicts parcel damage. Its data scientist, Tomás, reports 98% accuracy, but the IS auditor finds that one input is filled in only after a damage claim is filed, so the model sees the answer it should predict. The auditor reports that the figure cannot be relied on.

review: Compare training and test identifiers to detect people or records in both sets
Trace when the split was made relative to model tuning
Inspect input fields for information known only after the outcome
evidence: Overlap analysis of record and customer identifiers across splits
Split procedure with date, method and random seed
Test results on an out-of-time sample
audit_focus.recommend: Have the model owner rebuild the split by person or period and retest on truly unseen data.
audit_focus.decides: The model owner decides whether retested results meet the acceptance criteria

subtopics.isaca_rule: A score is only as good as its test data. Before relying on reported accuracy, confirm the test data was unseen: no shared people, future information or reuse for tuning.

exam_traps.trap: High accuracy on the test set proves the model is ready.
exam_traps.why: If test data leaked into training or tuning, the score measures memory, not new-case performance.

exam_traps.trap: A test set written by the model that generated the training data is unseen.
exam_traps.why: It shares the generator's phrasing and blind spots, flattering the score.

key_terms.definition: Information from the test set or the future reaching the model during training, inflating its scores.
Data kept aside and unseen during development, used once for the final performance check.
A test on data from a period after the training data, checking performance on newer cases.

topics.topic_name: AI Solution Development Methodologies and Lifecycle
topics.overview: AI systems pass through design, data, build or buy, validation, deployment, monitoring and retirement. This topic covers stage gates that stop a weak model from moving on, the documentation that makes a built or bought model auditable, and retiring a model without losing the records that explain its past decisions.
can_do: Name the evidence each AI lifecycle stage gate should require
Judge whether documentation is enough to assess a built, bought or tuned model
Plan what must be kept and what must be removed when a model is retired

subtopics.name: The AI Lifecycle and Stage Gates
subtopics.definition: The AI lifecycle runs from design through data, build, validation, deployment and monitoring to retirement, with stage gates requiring evidence before work moves on.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A model's behavior comes from its data, not just its code. Software-only gates can pass a model that is inaccurate, unfair or built on unfit data.
how_it_works: Before data gathering, design states purpose, users, people affected, success criteria and method; exact figures come from records.
MLOps automation should carry the gates, not skip them; approvers see source results beside each generated summary, since each can differ.

Each gate asks for evidence: data fitness (checked before training, since the model keeps what it learns), retrieved documents included, performance against agreed criteria, fairness results and owner sign-off.
Higher-impact uses get stricter gates and independent review; release also needs an owned monitoring plan with limits and a revalidation date, since models degrade unchanged.
A new use, or a live trial whose outputs take effect, re-enters the gates; unvalidated models run in shadow mode.
subtopics.example: A Dutch hospital trust's rostering team builds a nurse-staffing model. Nobody has recorded its intended use, who it affects or what error is acceptable. The IS auditor reports that the design gate was skipped, so later tests have no criteria to meet.

review: Walk a recent model release through each lifecycle gate and its evidence
Inspect release records for data and performance results, not only code tests
Compare gate strictness with the system's impact rating
evidence: Pipeline release logs showing which checks ran for each version
Signed gate approvals for each release, with approver and date
Training run records that reproduce the released version's results
audit_focus.recommend: Have the AI governance committee define lifecycle gates that require data and performance evidence, scaled to impact.
audit_focus.decides: The model owner approves each release under gate policy set by the AI governance committee

subtopics.isaca_rule: Treat a model as data plus code. Every gate demands evidence on data and model behavior, scaled to impact. Automation speeds the gates; it never removes them.

exam_traps.trap: If the code passes its tests, the retrained model is ready to release.
exam_traps.why: Identical code trained on different data behaves differently, so gates test results, not only software.

exam_traps.trap: Agile and MLOps teams move too fast for documentation.
exam_traps.why: Pipelines record evidence automatically; speed changes how it is captured, not whether it is needed.

key_terms.definition: A checkpoint where defined evidence must be shown and approved before work moves to the next lifecycle stage.
Machine learning operations: practices and tools that automate training, testing, deployment and monitoring of models.
Recording each training run's data, code, settings and results for reproduction.
A new model scores live cases beside the current one without its outputs deciding or being shown to deciders.
Removing what a model learned from specific records; deleting the records does not do it, so the usual route is retraining without them.

subtopics.name: Model Documentation and Build, Buy or Tune
subtopics.definition: Model documentation records what a model is for, what data trained it, how it was tested and its known limits; model cards and datasheets are common formats.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Without documentation, nobody can judge whether a model fits a new use or explain its decisions. Bought and pre-trained models need it too.
how_it_works: A model card gives uses, specific limits, training data and group results at the cutoff in use, with who set it and why; precision and recall hold only there.
Building allows full documentation; buying depends on vendor disclosure. A hosted model changes when its provider decides; any model knows nothing past its training data without a current source.
Tuning inherits the base model's unknowns and can weaken safety; open weights often carry their own license, apart from the code's.
Vendor contracts should require documentation, change notice, testing access, incident cooperation, training-input statistics for drift baselines and limits on training on customer data.
A tuned model can repeat any training file to any user, so it is as sensitive as its most restricted file.
subtopics.example: An Irish credit union plans to tune an open-source model to draft member letters. The model's public page lists no training data or known limits. The IS auditor reviews the selection checklist and reports that it accepts models without the information needed to judge their fitness or risk.

review: Inspect model cards for intended use, limits and performance by group
Compare contract terms with documentation and change-notice requirements
Trace a tuned model to its documented base model and version
evidence: Model cards and datasheets for in-scope models
Signed contracts with documentation, change-notice and audit clauses
Vendor due diligence records for each third-party model
audit_focus.recommend: Have procurement and the model owner make model documentation a contract condition before buying or tuning a model.
audit_focus.decides: The model owner decides to build, buy or tune, accepting residual risk within approved tolerances

subtopics.isaca_rule: No documentation, no reliance: built, bought or tuned, a model needs records of purpose, data, testing and limits, with limits flagged where users act. Vendor scores are inputs, not assurance.

exam_traps.trap: A vendor's model is the vendor's responsibility, so its documentation is the vendor's concern.
exam_traps.why: The organization using it answers for its decisions and needs documentation to judge fitness and explain outcomes.

exam_traps.trap: A language model's account of how it scored a case shows what drove the score.
exam_traps.why: It may not. Where people are owed reasons, faithful reasons are a selection requirement.

key_terms.definition: A short document describing a model's intended use, performance, training data and known limitations.
A document describing a dataset's origin, contents, collection method, intended uses and known gaps.
Further training a pre-trained model on new data to adapt it to a specific task.
The code, settings and data steps that turn data into a model; with the data, it allows rebuilding and retesting.

subtopics.name: Decommissioning AI Systems
subtopics.definition: Decommissioning retires an AI system in a controlled way: stopping its use, removing access and dependencies, and keeping the records needed to explain its past decisions.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Retired models may still need to explain decisions under appeal, audit or legal hold. Careless retirement destroys that evidence or leaves models, keys and data running.
how_it_works: Retirement, approved by the model owner, is triggered by replacement, poor performance retraining cannot fix, a changed purpose, regulation or expiring data rights, which reach models trained on the data.
Downstream systems, agents calling it as a tool (which may improvise) and models trained on its outputs are moved or rechecked; the manual fallback, staff skills included, is proven first.
Versions, inputs, outputs, decision logs and embedding indexes (inversion can recover much of their text) are kept while decisions can be challenged, then disposed of on schedule.
Access rights, credentials and application programming interface (API) keys are revoked, delegated access included; owners review jobs or rules the agent created elsewhere.
The AI inventory records status and kept records, with one entry per use, so retiring one use leaves others monitored; flawed outputs used as labels are withheld.
Retirement also covers training checkpoints, vendor-held copies of the model and tuning data, and saved memories, reviewed before moving to a successor; each gets a keep-or-delete decision.
subtopics.example: A Spanish city council switches off a parking-permit chatbot. The IS auditor finds its cloud endpoint still running with an active API key, and a payments system still calling it. The plan had no steps for access, dependencies or the inventory.

review: Compare the retirement plan with retention schedules and legal holds
Inspect the inventory and cloud accounts for retired models still running
Trace downstream calls to confirm dependencies moved before switch-off
evidence: Retention schedule entries for retired model records and legal holds
Access revocation records for endpoints, keys and service accounts
AI inventory entry marked retired, with the location of kept records
audit_focus.recommend: Have the model owner follow a retirement checklist covering records, access, dependencies and the inventory.
audit_focus.decides: The model owner approves retirement; legal counsel advises on retention and legal holds

subtopics.isaca_rule: Retiring a model ends its use, not its accountability. Keep what explains past decisions while they can be challenged, and remove everything else: access, keys, endpoints and dependencies. When choosing which of two models to retire, compare their errors for each group served.

exam_traps.trap: Keep the source code; past decisions can be regenerated if anyone asks.
exam_traps.why: Outputs depend on the trained model and data; without the exact version and inputs, past decisions cannot be reproduced.

key_terms.definition: An instruction to preserve records relevant to a dispute or investigation, overriding normal deletion schedules.
The network address where a deployed model takes requests.
A proven earlier model kept ready to run until its replacement performs well on live inputs.

topics.overview: AI systems change in more ways than ordinary software: retraining, new data, tuning, prompts, thresholds, settings and vendor updates all alter behavior. This topic covers which changes need control, how versions and configuration baselines make rollback possible, and how to control models a vendor can update.
can_do: Classify retraining, prompt, threshold and setting edits as changes needing control
Describe what a model version and configuration baseline must record
Recommend controls for vendor-hosted models that can update without notice

subtopics.name: What Counts as an AI Change
subtopics.definition: An AI change is any edit that can alter a system's outputs: new code, retraining, new data, fine-tuning, prompt or threshold edits, and configuration settings.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Many AI changes involve no code. If only code is controlled, a retrain or one-line prompt edit can change thousands of decisions unseen.
how_it_works: Retraining on fresh data makes a new model, even with identical code; trace changes from deployed versions, not commits.
Edits to a system prompt (automated rewrites included), threshold, quota or explanation component, or running at lower precision, can change outcomes as much as a code release.
Each change gets an impact assessment, testing against acceptance criteria, owner approval and a rollback plan, scaled to risk.
Routine retrains qualify as pre-approved standard changes only when preset, independently approved tests gate each run.
Fixes, bias fixes included, are changes; emergency ones may skip prior approval but are tested as time allows, documented and independently approved soon after.
Swapping a data source or feed, connecting a new tool or changing how reviewers see outputs alters what the system sees or does: a change even with the model unchanged.
subtopics.example: At a Polish bank's contact center, a supervisor lowers the score at which a sentiment model escalates calls. Nobody tests or approves the edit, and complaint handling slows for a week. The IS auditor finds that no sampled threshold or prompt edit went through change management.

review: Sample retraining, prompt and threshold edits and trace each to a change record
Compare deployed model versions and settings with approved change tickets
Inspect whether risk-based testing ran before each change went live
evidence: Deployment logs listing model versions, prompts and thresholds by date
Change tickets with test results and owner approval
Comparison of production settings against the approved baseline
audit_focus.recommend: Have IT management extend the change policy to retraining, prompt, threshold and setting changes, scaled to risk.
audit_focus.decides: The model owner approves each change within the change policy management sets

subtopics.isaca_rule: If it can change what the system decides, it is a change. Retraining, prompts, thresholds and settings need the same control as code, scaled to the decisions affected.

exam_traps.trap: Retraining with the same code is maintenance, not a change.
exam_traps.why: A retrained model is a new model and needs testing and approval like any release.

exam_traps.trap: Prompts are content, so business teams can edit them freely in production.
exam_traps.why: A system prompt steers what a generative system says and does, so edits need testing and approval.

key_terms.definition: Standing instructions given to a generative AI model that shape every answer it produces.
The score at which a model's output triggers an action, such as an alert, referral or decline.
Sending each request to one of several models by rule or AI judgment; changes test routing too.
A system or feed a model reads; its changes trigger AI review.

subtopics.name: Model Versioning, Configuration Baselines and Rollback
subtopics.definition: Model versioning gives every deployed model a unique identity tied to its trained artifact, code, data snapshot and settings; a configuration baseline is the approved state to compare against.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Without versions tied to their data and settings, nobody can reproduce a bad decision, prove which model made it or roll back to a version known to be sound.
how_it_works: A model registry keeps each model file, since retraining rarely rebuilds it exactly, with its code, data snapshot, settings, tests and approval; production loads a fixed approved version.
The configuration baseline covers model version, prompts, thresholds, feature settings and the model's libraries.
Production is compared with the baseline by version and settings records, since hosted models vary even at temperature 0; unexplained differences are investigated as unauthorized changes.
Rollback restores a previous approved version and its settings together, tested beforehand; models using its outputs, and versions tuned from a faulty one, are rechecked.
Decision logs record the model version behind each output, so decisions can be traced.
Releases go to a few users or sites first, test depth follows output change on fixed cases, and rollback fires on unusual model outputs, not only service errors.
subtopics.example: A Japanese e-commerce firm retrains its search-ranking model weekly. After a complaint, staff find the live ranking settings match no approved version in the registry. The IS auditor reports that settings changed outside change control and no tested rollback exists.

review: Compare production model versions and settings with the approved baseline
Trace a sample of decisions to the model version and data snapshot behind them
Inspect evidence that rollback was tested for critical models
evidence: Registry entries linking versions to data, code and approvals
Configuration comparison reports showing differences from baseline
Rollback test records with dates and results
audit_focus.recommend: Have the model owner keep a registry linking each version to its data, code and settings, with tested rollback.
audit_focus.decides: The model owner chooses the version in use and approves any rollback

subtopics.isaca_rule: A model version is the trained model plus the code, data and settings that produced it. Without all of them on record, it cannot be traced, explained or reliably rolled back.

exam_traps.trap: The source code repository is enough to track model versions.
exam_traps.why: Code history misses the data snapshot and settings; two models built from the same code can behave very differently.

exam_traps.trap: A hosted model's previous version is a lasting rollback target.
exam_traps.why: The vendor retires it on its own schedule, so the plan also needs a tested fallback.

key_terms.definition: A controlled store of model versions and their records.
The approved, documented set of settings and versions that production is compared against.
Restoring an earlier approved version and settings after a faulty change.
A fingerprint computed from a model's files that identifies the exact trained model, unlike a version label anyone can reuse.

subtopics.name: Vendor Model Updates
subtopics.definition: Vendor model updates are changes a provider makes to a hosted or embedded AI model, sometimes silently, that alter outputs inside the customer's processes.
subtopics.why_it_matters: When a provider swaps or retrains its model, the customer's decisions change without an internal change ticket, yet the organization answers for the outcomes.
how_it_works: Hosted services may update the model on their own schedule unless a version is pinned, and on-premises patches can carry new weights; a swapped embedding model needs every document reindexed.
Pinning holds the model, without new safety fixes, until the customer moves or the provider retires it; it does not freeze server-side filters, defaults or new features, such as memory.
Contracts can require notice, release notes, access to each new version before it applies, and the right to stay on a version for a set time.
Before adopting an update, the owner reruns regression tests covering agent actions, required refusals and required answers.
When one model serves several uses, each use's owner tests updates on its own work, using questions written in each language served; generated answers are tested for required content.
Monitoring output patterns, such as flag rates, detects silent changes contracts did not prevent; after updates, tests seek new error types too.
subtopics.example: A Mexican freight company's contract gives 30 days' notice and a test window before its vendor moves its invoice-reading model to a new version. The model owner skips regression tests, trusting release notes' accuracy claims. After the switch, new date formats make payments fail. The IS auditor reports that the notice term worked but the update was never tested on the company's invoices.

review: Inspect contracts for version pinning, update notice and testing rights
Compare vendor release notes with internal change and test records
Sample monitoring alerts for output shifts after vendor releases
evidence: Contract clauses on versions, notice and testing windows
Owner test results dated before each vendor update went live
Output monitoring trends around vendor release dates
audit_focus.recommend: Have procurement and the model owner secure version pinning or notice terms and require owner testing before updates.
audit_focus.decides: The model owner decides on adopting updates and accepts residual vendor risk within approved tolerances

subtopics.isaca_rule: A vendor's model update is a change to your system: pin versions or require notice, test before adoption and monitor for silent changes.

exam_traps.trap: The vendor tests its updates, so customers need not retest them.
exam_traps.why: The vendor tests its general model, not your prompts, data and thresholds; only your own tests show the effect.

key_terms.definition: Fixing a hosted AI service to one stable version, not a preview that can change anytime, so behavior changes only by decision.
Rerunning fixed cases with known expected results to detect unwanted changes.
Values sent with each request, such as temperature (higher gives more varied output) and maximum length (too low cuts answers off).

topics.topic_name: Supervision of AI Solutions (e.g., outputs, impacts, and decisions)
topics.overview: Once deployed, an AI system needs people who watch what it decides and what those decisions do to people and connected systems. This topic covers human oversight that works, monitoring of drift, performance and impacts with AI-specific KPIs and KRIs, and decision logs and appeal routes for affected people.
can_do: Tell effective human oversight from rubber-stamping
Choose KPIs and KRIs that show decision quality and drift, not just uptime
Check that affected people can appeal an AI decision to a person with authority

subtopics.name: Human Oversight and Automation Bias
subtopics.definition: Human oversight means people who understand an AI system can monitor it, override its decisions and stop it, at a level matched to the decision's impact.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A reviewer who approves everything gives the look of control without the substance. Automation bias, the habit of trusting machine output too much, turns human review into a rubber stamp.
how_it_works: The oversight model is chosen by impact: the more a decision affects people's rights or money, the closer the human.
Effective reviewers have training, the skill to decide cases unaided, time per case, the reasons and any filled-in inputs behind each output and authority to override without penalty.
Override rates, reasons and review times are tracked, analyzed and fed back into monitoring; reviewing AI-written notices about a decision is not reviewing the decision.
Near-zero overrides combined with very short review times suggest rubber-stamping rather than judgment; people on the loop watch only as many systems as they can take over in time.
Showing a model's output before reviewers judge anchors them; recording their own judgment first keeps the review independent.
Reasons shown beside outputs can deepen automation bias; if agreement rises even on wrong outputs, reasons persuade rather than inform.

types.meaning: A person approves each decision before it takes effect; suited to high-impact decisions about people.
The system acts on its own while a person monitors it and can intervene or stop it.
People set policy, limits and shutdown conditions without reviewing individual decisions.

subtopics.example: At an Australian state transport agency, officers confirm an AI model's suggested license suspensions. Their screen shows only the model's score, not why it was given, and reversing a suggestion needs a manager's written sign-off. The IS auditor observes live reviews and reports that the design leaves officers unable to understand or challenge the model.

review: Observe reviewers handling live cases and time their reviews
Analyze override rates and reasons by reviewer and period
Compare the oversight model in use with the decision's impact rating
evidence: Decision logs showing reviewer, time taken and any override
Override analysis reports with reasons and follow-up
Reviewer training records and documented override authority
audit_focus.recommend: Have the model owner give reviewers time, reasons and override authority, and analyze overrides regularly.
audit_focus.decides: The model owner sets the oversight model within AI policy and the AI governance committee's standards

subtopics.isaca_rule: Oversight must work, not just exist. For high-impact decisions, a person must understand the output, have time to judge it and be able to override or stop the system. Very high agreement with very little review time is a warning sign, not reassurance.

exam_traps.trap: A human signs off every decision, so oversight is in place.
exam_traps.why: Sign-off without time, reasons or authority to disagree is a rubber stamp. Test how reviewers actually behave, not just that they exist.

key_terms.definition: The tendency to over-trust automated output and accept it without enough scrutiny.
The share of AI outputs that human reviewers change or reject.
Review by a person who understands a case and can override and answer for it; a model checking a model is not oversight.

subtopics.name: Monitoring Drift, Performance and Impacts
subtopics.definition: AI monitoring tracks a deployed system's inputs, outputs, accuracy, fairness and effects on people and connected systems against tolerances, so decay is caught early.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Models decay silently as the world changes; a fully available system can decide worse, so uptime says nothing about decision quality.
how_it_works: Drift needs no code change: inputs shift (data drift) or their link to outcomes changes (concept drift); comparing inputs with training data also catches blank, default-filled or stuck feeds.

Key performance indicators (KPIs) track value, such as accuracy and, where probabilities set amounts, calibration against actual rates; key risk indicators (KRIs) track drift, group error rates and complaints.

Each indicator has a threshold the owner sets within senior management's tolerance; a breach triggers review, retraining through change control or disengagement; monitors change with each release's inputs.
Impacts are monitored too: how people use the system, effects on people and connected systems, and energy and resource use; a random comparison group shows what the model's choices add.
Trend reports go to the owner and, for high-impact systems, the AI governance committee and board; a rarer target event lowers precision even without drift.
When true outcomes arrive late, input and prediction drift act as early warnings; a sudden unexplained gain can signal leakage.
subtopics.example: A Singapore port operator uses a model to predict crane maintenance needs. Its dashboard shows 99.9% availability, but technicians report more surprise breakdowns since new crane types arrived. The IS auditor compares last year's predictions with actual failures and reports that no indicator tracks accuracy or input drift.

review: Reperform a sample of recent predictions against actual outcomes
Compare KRIs and tolerances with the risks in the impact assessment
Trace tolerance breaches to the review or action they triggered
evidence: Production accuracy and drift metrics trended since deployment
KPI and KRI reports showing tolerances, owner thresholds and trends
Tickets showing action taken on each tolerance breach
audit_focus.recommend: Have the model owner add drift, accuracy and impact indicators with thresholds that trigger review and reporting.
audit_focus.decides: The model owner sets use-level thresholds within tolerances senior management sets under board-approved appetite

subtopics.isaca_rule: Monitor decisions, not just servers. Ask what would tell the owner, in time, that decisions had worsened or turned unfair, and what happens next.

exam_traps.trap: Stable accuracy on the original test set shows the model is not drifting.
exam_traps.why: The original test set reflects launch conditions. Drift shows in production data and outcomes, so measure it there.

exam_traps.trap: Retraining on a fixed schedule replaces the need to monitor.
exam_traps.why: Scheduled retraining shows nothing about decision quality and can bake in bad data.

key_terms.definition: A change in the inputs a model receives compared with its training data.
A change in the relationship between inputs and the correct outcome, so learned patterns stop holding.
A measure warning that a risk nears or passes tolerance.

subtopics.name: Decision Logs, Appeals and Feedback
subtopics.definition: Decision logs record what an AI system decided, on which inputs and model version; appeal routes let affected people challenge a decision before a person with authority.
subtopics.why_it_matters: People harmed by a wrong automated decision need a way to correct it; without logs and appeals, errors stay hidden and harm continues.
how_it_works: Each logged decision records inputs, model version, output (any AI draft and the text as sent), human review and final action; ranked allocations keep the full ranking and cutoff.
Affected people are told an automated system was involved, the reasons that drove the decision, and how to challenge it; generated wording is checked against logged factors.
Appeals reach a person who can review and reverse the decision, not just rerun the model; affected communities get a reviewed route; chat verdicts people act on count as decisions.
Appeals, complaints and overrides are studied by model version for patterns pointing to model errors.
Logs are kept long enough for appeals, complaints and regulators, with access limited; appeal staff see each case's inputs and factors, not a bare score.
Before a model retrains on its own past decisions, appeals and overrides won on its errors, not on new evidence, correct the labels.
subtopics.example: A German housing association ranks social-housing applicants with a model. Rejected applicants can email a general inbox, but no one may change a ranking. The IS auditor traces sampled complaints and finds none reached anyone able to reverse a ranking.

review: Trace a sample of appeals from receipt to final outcome
Confirm reviewers hold documented authority to reverse decisions
Compare appeal reversal rates with model monitoring reports
evidence: System decision log entries for sampled appeal cases
Appeal register with dates, reviewer and outcome
Reports showing appeal trends used in model monitoring
audit_focus.recommend: Have the model owner provide an appeal route to staff who can reverse decisions, and track appeal outcomes.
audit_focus.decides: The model owner decides reversals under the appeal policy management sets

subtopics.isaca_rule: Every high-impact AI decision must be explainable from its log and open to appeal before a person who can change it; appeals also reveal errors metrics miss.

exam_traps.trap: Publishing how the model works gives affected people enough protection.
exam_traps.why: Transparency helps but corrects nothing; people need a route to someone who can review and reverse the decision.

exam_traps.trap: Once an appeal is upheld, the case is settled.
exam_traps.why: The model's next run can reimpose the decision. An upheld appeal holds unless new evidence arrives; otherwise automation overrules the reviewer.

key_terms.definition: A record of each automated decision with its inputs, model version, output and final action.
A defined way for an affected person to challenge an AI decision before someone with authority to change it.
A record of which documents or passages, by version, a generative system retrieved for each answer.

topics.overview: Testing shows whether an AI system works as intended, for everyone it affects, and under pressure. This topic covers test, evaluation, verification and validation (TEVV) against criteria set in advance, fairness testing across groups, and independent validation, robustness testing and red teaming.
can_do: Check that acceptance criteria were set before testing began
Ask for results broken out by group, not one overall figure
Judge whether validation is independent of the model builders

subtopics.name: TEVV and Acceptance Criteria
subtopics.definition: Test, evaluation, verification and validation (TEVV) are the activities that show an AI system meets its requirements, judged against acceptance criteria agreed before testing.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Criteria chosen after results can pass anything; tests on unrealistic data, or only pre-launch, mislead.
how_it_works: Acceptance criteria cover accuracy, fairness, robustness and explainability, trace to the business need and senior management's tolerances, and measure any staff baseline under normal working conditions.

Verification shows the system meets its specification; validation shows it fits its intended use, tested with domain experts on data and conditions like deployment, including holdout and out-of-time samples.
Test sets, metrics, tools and results are documented for rerunning; a model that refers decisions is judged on accuracy and referral rate together.
Testing continues after launch through monitoring and periodic revalidation, not only at release; grading models, which can favor longer answers, are checked against experts before their marks count.
Generative AI is tested by human review of scenario sets, out-of-scope requests and cited sources included, for accuracy, harm and confabulation, each case run several times, raters blind to version.
A compressed, quantized or converted model is a new version; acceptance tests are rerun on the form that will run, with any new component feeding it, such as speech recognition.
subtopics.example: A Chilean water regulator's billing-error model has a test plan naming accuracy as the only measure, with no pass mark. Comparing it with the impact assessment, the IS auditor reports that a pass mark and limits on false flags against households must be agreed before testing.

review: Compare the date criteria were approved with the date testing began
Inspect test data for similarity to production conditions
Reperform a sample of cases from the documented test set
evidence: Reperformance results on a sample of documented test cases
Signed criteria document dated before the first test run
Test plan and results with data description and metrics
audit_focus.recommend: Have the model owner approve acceptance criteria from business need, within approved tolerances, before testing begins.
audit_focus.decides: The model owner decides whether results meet the criteria for release

subtopics.isaca_rule: Set the bar before the jump. Criteria come from need and risk tolerance and are fixed before testing; tests use deployment-like data and continue after launch.

exam_traps.trap: The model owner can adjust the pass mark once results show what is achievable.
exam_traps.why: Criteria moved after results fit the model, not the need; changes need a documented reason and approval.

key_terms.definition: Test, evaluation, verification and validation: the activities that show an AI system meets its requirements.
Measurable conditions, agreed in advance, that a system must meet before it is accepted.
A generative AI system producing confident but false or invented content.
Testing how an AI system, especially an agent, behaves when tools or inputs fail; agents are judged on every action, not just the end result.

subtopics.name: Fairness Testing Across Groups
subtopics.definition: Fairness testing compares an AI system's outcomes and error rates across groups of people, such as age, gender, ethnicity or region, to find unequal harm.
subtopics.why_it_matters: One overall figure can hide much worse results for a smaller group, harming people and breaching anti-discrimination law.
how_it_works: Results are broken out by group and combined group, such as age with language, with enough cases: approval or flag rates, false positives and negatives, accuracy and error direction.
Fairness measures can conflict; the owner chooses and documents which apply, with reasons and legal input; where scores set graded amounts, outcomes in each band are compared by group.
Proxy variables, such as a postal code standing in for ethnicity, can carry bias even with protected attributes left out; fixes count only if the live system applies them.
Fairness is tested before launch, in live use and after each retrain, since clicks a ranking drives can widen a gap; for rankings, at the top positions people choose from.
Where group data is not collected, the organization documents how it will estimate fairness lawfully; voluntary answers may not represent the whole group.
For generative AI, paired prompts differing only in a personal signal, such as a name or language, are run many times; for images, many outputs per prompt show stereotyped portrayal.
subtopics.example: A Vietnamese telehealth service's symptom checker advises patients whether to see a doctor; its validation report gives one overall missed-urgent rate. Results the IS auditor requests by age band and app language show older Khmer-language users told to stay home twice as often when they needed care. The auditor reports the gap.

review: Reperform fairness metrics by group on a sample of decisions
Compare chosen fairness measures with the documented rationale and legal advice
Inspect model inputs for proxies of protected characteristics
evidence: Auditor-recomputed error rates for each group from sampled decisions
Fairness measure selection record with legal and ethics input
Production fairness monitoring trends since release
audit_focus.recommend: Have the model owner test and monitor outcomes and errors by group against documented fairness criteria.
audit_focus.decides: The model owner, advised by legal counsel, decides whether disparities are acceptable within approved tolerances

subtopics.isaca_rule: Ask whose errors an average hides. Expect group-level results, a documented reason for the fairness measures chosen and the same checks in production.

exam_traps.trap: Removing gender and ethnicity from the inputs makes the model fair.
exam_traps.why: Other inputs, such as postal code or work history, can act as proxies. Only testing outcomes by group shows whether bias remains.

key_terms.definition: Performance figures broken out by group instead of reported as one overall number.
An input that closely tracks a protected characteristic and can carry its bias into a model.
Bias in the outcomes a model learns from and is tested against, such as skewed past ratings; fairness measured against them inherits it.

subtopics.name: Independent Validation, Robustness and Red Teaming
subtopics.definition: Independent validation is review and retesting of a model by people separate from its builders; robustness testing and red teaming probe how it behaves under stress or attack.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Builders share the model's assumptions and want it to pass. Without independent and adversarial testing, blind spots and weaknesses reach production unnoticed.
how_it_works: Validators are independent of the development team and have skills suited to the model type, such as generative AI, and access to review design, data, code and results.
Validation covers soundness of the approach, data, performance, fairness, explainability and limits.

Robustness testing feeds noisy, unfamiliar, reworded, reordered and deliberately crafted inputs, such as keyword stuffing, and checks outputs stay stable or are referred; uses beyond training range get stress tests.
Red teaming has testers act as attackers or misusers of the system as deployed, with its tools, data sources and the system prompts clients may write.
Red teaming covers every language and channel served, as safeguards can be weaker in some languages.
subtopics.example: A Korean marine insurer's hull-claims model passed independent validation at launch. A year later, actuaries retrained it with a new data source covering Arctic routes and released it after checking only overall accuracy. The IS auditor's review of release records finds validation not repeated after a material change and no robustness testing on unusual voyage data.

review: Compare validator names with the development team roster
Inspect validation scope for data, fairness, robustness and limits
Trace red-team findings to fixes or formally accepted risks
evidence: Independent validation report with scope, findings and validator roles
Robustness and red-team results with severity ratings
Remediation tracker linking findings to owners and dates
audit_focus.recommend: Have management assign validators independent of the builders and require robustness testing scaled to impact.
audit_focus.decides: The model owner decides on release; management accepts any unremediated findings

subtopics.isaca_rule: Builders do not grade their own model. Expect validation by people independent of development, testing under stress and attack, and revalidation after material change. The IS auditor assesses that validation and never performs or approves it; the IS auditor's probing tests are audit evidence, not a substitute.

exam_traps.trap: The IS auditor should validate the model because auditors are independent.
exam_traps.why: Validating or approving the model would make the IS auditor part of the control; management arranges validation.

exam_traps.trap: Passing a public jailbreak library shows a model resists jailbreaks.
exam_traps.why: Models are often trained against public attack lists, so a pass can come from memory; red teams add fresh attacks.

key_terms.definition: Review and retesting of a model by qualified people who did not build it.
Structured testing in which people act as attackers or misusers to find weaknesses, repeated as the system and attack methods change.
A model's ability to keep producing reliable outputs when inputs are noisy, unusual or manipulated.

topics.topic_name: Threats and Vulnerabilities specific to AI
topics.overview: AI adds attack surfaces that ordinary security controls miss: training data, model files, prompts, retrieved content and the tools agents can use. Using the NIST adversarial machine learning taxonomy and MITRE ATLAS, this topic covers attacks on data and models, prompt injection, and identity and access management for models and agents.
can_do: Match poisoning, evasion, extraction and inference attacks to scenarios
Tell direct from indirect prompt injection and rank their risk
Evaluate least privilege for models, keys and agent tools

subtopics.name: Attacks on Data and Models
subtopics.definition: Attacks on data and models target how AI learns or answers: poisoning corrupts training, evasion fools a trained model, and extraction or inference steals the model or its data.
subtopics.why_it_matters: These attacks arrive through normal data feeds and queries, so perimeter controls rarely see them. A poisoned or copied model can fail, leak data or lose value without any breach.
how_it_works: Poisoning is countered by provenance checks, limits on who adds training data or feedback, and anomaly checks; clean-label poison passes label review, and federated learning's secure aggregation hides poisoned updates.

Extraction, membership inference (learning whether a person's data trained it) and reconstruction, including memorized text a tuned model repeats, are slowed by query limits and monitoring; coarser outputs hinder evasion.
Downloaded models, libraries, datasets and data fetched by link (lapsed domains can be bought) stay untrusted until verified; some model formats run code when opened, so isolate even signed files.
An AI threat model covers data, model files, interfaces, suppliers and self-supplied enrollment images, morphable to match two people; leaked models let attackers rehearse evasions offline.
Backdoor poisoning plants a hidden trigger during training; the model behaves normally on ordinary tests, so uninspectable training data is a risk in itself.
The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) taxonomy NIST AI 100-2e2025 sorts attacks by attacker goal, access, knowledge and lifecycle stage; MITRE ATLAS lists real techniques.

types.meaning: Planting or altering training data, or tampering with a model, so it learns wrong or hidden behavior or degrades for all users.
Crafting inputs at use time that a trained model gets wrong, such as a disguised fraud pattern.
Querying a model repeatedly and using its answers to build a working copy.

types.term: Membership inference and data reconstruction (model inversion)
types.meaning: Using a model's outputs to learn whether a record was in its training data, or to reconstruct that data.
Tampered models, libraries or datasets obtained from outside sources.

subtopics.example: A Turkish e-commerce platform's image model blocks counterfeit listings. Sellers discover that small stickers placed over a logo let fakes pass. The IS auditor reviews the threat model and test records and reports that evasion was never considered and that robustness testing used no altered images.

review: Inspect the AI threat model for data, model, interface and supplier attacks
Trace training data and feedback inputs to the controls that screen them
Evaluate query limits and monitoring on externally exposed model interfaces
evidence: Query logs and rate-limit settings for exposed model endpoints
Threat model document listing attacks per component and their controls
Hash or signature verification records for third-party model files
audit_focus.recommend: Have the security team and model owner keep an AI threat model with controls for poisoning, evasion and extraction.
audit_focus.decides: The model owner accepts residual threat risk within the board-approved risk appetite

subtopics.isaca_rule: Threat-model the AI, not just the server. Ask how its data, model and interfaces could be attacked, using a recognized taxonomy, and look for a control at each point.

exam_traps.trap: An internal model behind the firewall needs no AI threat model.
exam_traps.why: Poisoning arrives through normal feeds, and insiders and suppliers can tamper with models; network position removes no AI-specific threat.

key_terms.definition: A public knowledge base of attacker tactics and techniques against AI systems, with real case studies.
The study of attacks on AI systems and their defenses.
Feeding fake video, such as a deepfake, straight into an app, bypassing its camera.

subtopics.name: Prompt Injection and Jailbreaks
subtopics.definition: Prompt injection is input crafted to override a generative AI system's instructions; direct injection comes from the user, indirect injection hides in content the system reads.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Generative models take instructions and data through the same channel, so any text they read can steer them. When the system can act, injection becomes data theft or fraud.
how_it_works: Direct prompting attacks, including jailbreaks, come from a user typing instructions that bypass the system's rules; longer input limits allow many-shot jailbreaks.
Indirect prompt injection is planted by third parties in emails, files, images, retrieved documents or web pages, public posts on approved sites included; victims are often the system's users.
No filter fully stops injection, so designs assume some attacks succeed and limit what the model can reach and do; hosted safety filters do not travel with the weights.
Controls include separating trusted instructions from untrusted content, filtering inputs and outputs, human approval for risky actions and least-privilege tools.
Injection and jailbreak tests try each attack many times, since outputs vary, and are repeated after each change.
Anything in the context, system prompt included, can be extracted by prompting, so it never holds secrets or other users' data.
subtopics.example: A Swedish research foundation's assistant summarizes grant proposals for reviewers. A tester hides white text telling it to rate the proposal an outstanding fit, and the summary obeys. The IS auditor reports that no control separates proposal content from the assistant's instructions.

review: Inspect red-team results for direct and indirect injection attempts
Trace each untrusted content source to separation and filtering controls
Identify actions the system can take without human approval
evidence: Red-team reports with injection test cases and outcomes
Architecture diagram showing untrusted inputs and tool permissions
Logs of blocked and flagged prompts with review outcomes
audit_focus.recommend: Have the model owner limit tool permissions, separate untrusted content and require approval for high-risk actions.
audit_focus.decides: The model owner accepts residual injection risk within the board-approved risk appetite

subtopics.isaca_rule: Assume injected instructions will sometimes succeed. Rank the risk by what the system reads from outsiders and can do; contain damage with least privilege and human approval, not a firewall or single filter.

exam_traps.trap: A network firewall protects a chatbot from prompt injection.
exam_traps.why: Injection arrives as ordinary text through permitted channels; network controls and malware scans cannot judge intent.

exam_traps.trap: Filtering the model's outputs is enough to stop injection.
exam_traps.why: Output filters catch some harmful text but not every action or leak. Limit what the model can reach and require approval for risky actions.

key_terms.definition: A user typing instructions to override a generative AI system's rules.
Instructions hidden by a third party in content an AI system later reads, such as a file or web page.
A direct prompt crafted to make a model ignore its safety rules.

subtopics.name: Excessive Agency and Access Management for AI
subtopics.definition: Excessive agency is an AI agent having more tools, permissions or autonomy than its task needs; identity and access management (IAM) for AI keeps each agent to the minimum.
subtopics.why_it_matters: An agent is only as safe as its permissions: manipulated or wrong, it can harm whatever its account reaches.
how_it_works: Each agent and model has its own identity, never a shared or personal account; records name the person an agent acts for.

Tools follow least privilege: an approved list the agent cannot extend, read-only where possible, narrow scopes, parameters such as recipients fixed from records, no standing payment or account-change rights.
High-impact actions, such as payments or deletions, need human approval the model cannot grant itself; value limits bind totals across tools, so splitting or switching tools cannot evade them.
Application programming interface (API) keys and credentials sit in a vault the tools use, never in prompts the model could repeat; AI-generated code runs sandboxed without them.
Model files, training data and prompts are access-controlled too; an agent never holds write access to its own instructions or permissions.
Owners review agents' rights, including those held through tool keys, and monitor their actions, since a steered agent misuses rights it legitimately holds.
subtopics.example: A Moroccan furniture retailer's delivery-rescheduling agent runs under a developer's personal account that can read all customer records and edit staff rosters. The IS auditor reports the excess rights and that no access review covers non-human accounts.

review: Compare each agent's permissions and tools with its documented tasks
Inspect access reviews for agent and model service accounts
Sample agent payment or deletion actions and trace each to an approval record
evidence: Access listings for agent and model identities with owners
Tool configuration showing scopes granted to each agent
Secrets vault records of key rotation and access
audit_focus.recommend: Have the model owner restrict agent identities to needed tools, require approval for high-impact actions and review access regularly.
audit_focus.decides: The model owner approves agent permissions; management accepts residual access risk within the board-approved risk appetite

subtopics.isaca_rule: Judge an agent by what its account can do, not by its instructions: instructions can be overridden; permissions hold.

exam_traps.trap: Telling the agent in its prompt not to take risky actions is an adequate control.
exam_traps.why: Injection or error can override instructions; access rights hold whatever the model is told.

exam_traps.trap: Broad standing permissions make an agent more useful, so they are justified.
exam_traps.why: Unneeded rights turn any manipulation or error into real damage.

key_terms.definition: A system using a model to plan and act through tools.
An account used by software, such as a service or agent, not a person.
The exact action and values an approver sees from the tool layer before an agent acts, not the agent's own summary.
A network rule letting an agent connect only to approved destinations, so planted links cannot reach internal systems.

topics.topic_name: Incident Response Management specific to AI
topics.overview: AI incidents include harmful, biased or wrong outputs, data leakage, manipulation and drift beyond tolerance, not only security breaches. This topic covers recognizing and triaging them by impact on people, containing them by disengaging or rolling back while preserving evidence, and making sure the root cause is removed: through problem management for faults, and before closure when the incident is manipulation such as poisoning.
can_do: Recognize an AI incident from complaints, monitoring alerts or reports
Order containment, evidence preservation and root cause analysis correctly
Assess whether problem management fixes the cause, not just the symptom

subtopics.name: Recognizing and Triaging AI Incidents
subtopics.definition: An AI incident is an event where an AI system causes or nearly causes harm: wrong, biased or unsafe outputs, data leakage, manipulation or performance beyond tolerance.
subtopics.why_it_matters: AI failures often look like ordinary complaints or odd metrics, not alarms. If they are not recognized and triaged as incidents, harm to people can continue for weeks.
how_it_works: Detection channels include monitoring alerts, tolerance breaches, user complaints, staff reports, override spikes, safeguard activations, appeals, red-team findings, vendor notices and unexplained output shifts, even welcome ones.
The incident policy defines AI incidents explicitly, so service desk and complaint staff know when to escalate.
Triage ranks first by impact on people, including through internal tools whose outputs reach them, then on the business, and by how many decisions are affected.
Roles are named in advance: the model owner, technical responders, domain experts who can judge harm, privacy and legal staff, and communications.
An AI incident may also be a security, privacy or safety incident, and is coordinated with those processes, not forced into one.
One leaked or wrong answer can repeat for many users through shared caches, prompts or models, so linked incidents are triaged together; personal-data disclosures bring in privacy staff at once.
subtopics.example: A Philippine mobile operator's AI chatbot starts telling customers that a fee waiver program has ended when it has not. Over two weeks, the complaints team logs 300 calls about it as routine service questions. The IS auditor traces the complaints and finds no route for staff to raise AI output problems as incidents.

review: Trace sampled AI-related complaints to see whether they became incidents
Inspect the incident policy for an AI incident definition and triage criteria
Compare detection channels in the plan with those actually monitored
evidence: Complaint and service desk records tagged to AI systems
Incident register entries for AI events with triage ratings
Incident policy with AI definitions, severity criteria and named roles
audit_focus.recommend: Have the incident manager define AI incidents, add complaint and monitoring channels, and triage by impact on people.
audit_focus.decides: The incident manager sets severity; the model owner or a pre-delegated incident commander decides to disengage

subtopics.isaca_rule: AI incidents are not only security incidents. Wrong, biased or harmful outputs and drift beyond tolerance count too. Look for a definition, detection channels that include complaints, triage by impact on people and named roles.

exam_traps.trap: An AI problem is an incident only if there was a security breach.
exam_traps.why: Biased decisions, harmful advice and drift beyond tolerance harm people without any breach. Each needs incident handling, as does one serious harm within tolerance.

key_terms.definition: An event in which an AI system causes or nearly causes harm through its outputs, data or behavior.
Ranking incidents by severity and impact to decide response order and escalation.

subtopics.name: Containment: Disengage, Roll Back and Preserve Evidence
subtopics.definition: Containing an AI incident means stopping further harm, by disengaging the system, pausing its actions or rolling back, while preserving the evidence needed to find the cause.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A harmful model keeps deciding until someone stops it, but restarting, retraining or deleting logs early can destroy needed evidence.
how_it_works: Disengagement mechanisms (a kill switch, a tested manual fallback, not an untested substitute model) are set before deployment; poisoned data is quarantined and its retrains held.
Rollback restores an approved version, pausing live learning; it contains, not fixes, and cannot undo drift older versions share.
Preserved evidence covers inputs, outputs, prompts, model and data versions, configuration and logs, with chain of custody; generative outputs cannot be reliably regenerated.
Decision logs identify affected people so harm is assessed and remedied; disengaging also cuts manual paths to the model and holds outputs still queued.
Disengaging an agent suspends its credentials, tools, jobs and anything it created elsewhere; tampered memories and settings are restored from clean copies.
Memorized leaks need disengagement or rollback; deleting source files cannot unteach a model; filters can miss rewording; leaked models cannot be recalled, so reduce reliance on them.
subtopics.example: A Danish pharmacy chain's drug-interaction model stops warning pharmacists about a common combination after an update, and an engineer retrains it overnight. The IS auditor finds the faulty version and logs overwritten and reports that no one had authority to disengage the model or preserve evidence.

review: Inspect disengagement mechanisms and named authority for each high-impact model
Trace a past AI incident to confirm evidence was preserved before changes
Walk through a rollback or fallback exercise and its results
evidence: Evidence store contents for a past incident, matched to its timeline
Tested kill-switch or fallback procedures with dates and owners
Custody log showing who accessed incident evidence and when
audit_focus.recommend: Have the model owner assign disengagement authority, test fallbacks and preserve inputs, outputs and versions before any fix.
audit_focus.decides: The model owner or a pre-delegated incident commander decides to disengage; the incident manager directs containment

subtopics.isaca_rule: Stop the harm, keep the evidence, then fix: disengage or roll back when people are harmed, preserve evidence before any change, and treat rollback as containment, not the fix.

exam_traps.trap: Retrain the model at once to fix the faulty behavior.
exam_traps.why: Retraining before the cause is known may repeat the fault and overwrites evidence; contain first, then investigate.

exam_traps.trap: Delete incident logs quickly because they contain personal data.
exam_traps.why: They are needed to find the cause and remedy harm; restrict them, then dispose of them on schedule.

key_terms.definition: A tested way to quickly stop an AI system or its actions.
A record of who handled evidence and when, showing it is unaltered.
The earlier version restored; after poisoning, it must predate the poisoned data.
Hosted AI records kept only until the provider's retention ends or next update; request preservation at once.

subtopics.name: Root Cause, Problem Management and Reporting
subtopics.definition: Root cause analysis for AI finds why an incident happened, in the data, model, prompt, integration or oversight, so problem management can stop it from recurring.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Patching a prompt or rolling back treats the symptom. If poisoned data, weak change control or a missing tolerance remains, the same failure returns at the next retraining or update.
how_it_works: Investigators compare preserved inputs, outputs and versions with the last good state; a vendor's fault still leaves the organization's own gap to record.

Causes are traced across layers: data (drift, which arrives with no new version; poisoning; labeling; coverage gaps behind 'edge cases'), retrieved content, model, prompt or configuration, integration and oversight.
Once service is restored, a problem record carries the cause; the fix, a control outside the model where possible, goes through change control and is checked to work.
Incidents are reported to owners, the AI governance committee and, where required, regulators, affected people and customers who relied on the outputs.
Causes include training signals that reward harm and AI answers copied into its sources; lessons, such as slow detection, update threat models, tolerances, tests and training.
A vendor-side cause with a distant fix stays open as a known error, with a tested workaround outside the model; human-check workarounds can decay into rubber stamps.
subtopics.example: An Indian education company's essay-scoring model began marking one region's essays lower. Engineers adjusted the prompt and closed the ticket; at the next retraining, the gap returned. The IS auditor reports that no problem record was opened, so no root cause analysis examined the training data and the fix treated only the symptom.

review: Sample closed AI incidents and check each has a linked problem record
Compare problem records with later recurrences of the same failure
Inspect reports to owners and regulators for timeliness and completeness
evidence: Root cause analysis records naming the failing layer
Problem register linking causes to changes and verification
Incident reports sent to owners, committees and regulators
audit_focus.recommend: Have the problem manager link every AI incident of unknown cause to a problem register entry tracked to a tested fix.
audit_focus.decides: The model owner decides remediation; management decides external reporting with legal counsel

subtopics.isaca_rule: A rollback or prompt patch restores service; it does not remove the cause. An ordinary fault's incident may close once service is confirmed, while a problem record carries the cause to a verified fix. Suspected manipulation, such as poisoning, stays open until the cause is removed.

exam_traps.trap: Once outputs return to normal after a rollback, the AI failure is resolved.
exam_traps.why: Rollback restores service but the cause can return at the next retraining; a problem record, or for manipulation an open security incident, carries it to a fix.

key_terms.definition: A structured investigation finding an incident's underlying reason, not just its symptoms.
The process that finds and removes incident causes so they do not recur.

key_terminologies.Data lineage: The recorded path of data from its source through every transformation into a model.
key_terminologies.Data leakage: Test or future information reaching a model during training, inflating its reported scores.
key_terminologies.Representativeness: How closely training data matches the people and conditions a model will serve.
key_terminologies.Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): A design in which a generative model looks up documents at answer time.
key_terminologies.Stage gate: A lifecycle checkpoint where evidence must be shown and approved before work moves on.
key_terminologies.MLOps: Machine learning operations: automated training, testing, deployment and monitoring of models.
key_terminologies.Model card: A document describing a model's intended use, data, performance and known limits.
key_terminologies.Model registry: A controlled store of model versions with their data, code, settings and approvals.
key_terminologies.Version pinning: Fixing a hosted AI service to one model version so behavior changes only by decision.
key_terminologies.Human-in-the-loop: A person approves each AI decision before it takes effect.
key_terminologies.Automation bias: Over-trusting automated output and accepting it without enough scrutiny.
key_terminologies.Data drift: A change in the inputs a model receives compared with its training data.
key_terminologies.Concept drift: A change in the link between inputs and the correct outcome.
key_terminologies.Key risk indicator (KRI): A measure that warns when a risk is rising toward its tolerance.
key_terminologies.Appeal route: A way for an affected person to challenge an AI decision before someone who can change it.
key_terminologies.TEVV: Test, evaluation, verification and validation of an AI system.
key_terminologies.Fairness testing: Comparing a system's outcomes and error rates across groups of people.
key_terminologies.Independent validation: Review and retesting of a model by qualified people who did not build it.
key_terminologies.Red teaming: Testing in which people act as attackers or misusers to find weaknesses.
key_terminologies.Poisoning: Corrupting training data or a model so it learns wrong or hidden behavior.
key_terminologies.Evasion: Crafting inputs that a trained model gets wrong at use time.
key_terminologies.Model extraction: Rebuilding a working copy of a model from its query responses.
key_terminologies.Prompt injection: Input crafted to override a generative AI system's instructions, typed directly or hidden in content it reads.
key_terminologies.Excessive agency: An AI agent having more tools, permissions or autonomy than its task needs.
key_terminologies.AI incident: An event in which an AI system causes or nearly causes harm.
key_terminologies.Kill switch: A tested mechanism that quickly stops an AI system or its automated actions.
key_terminologies.Root cause analysis: An investigation that finds the underlying reason for an incident, not just its symptoms.
